title: How Boycotts Work (Or Do They?)
summary: Josh and Chuck explore how boycotts work, starting with the origin of the word in Charles Cunningham Boycott's 1879 County Mayo eviction fight and Father O'Malley's verb use. They cover what makes a boycott effective (clear goal, narrow target, core customers, substitutability, hitting the bottom line, observability), walk through historical boycotts (American colonial non-importation and the Boston Tea Party, the Free Produce Movement, the Montgomery bus boycott, the grape boycott, the anti-apartheid boycott and Sun City album, the North Carolina bathroom bill boycott), and then look at social media boycotts and counter-"buycotts" (Goya, Nike, Bud Light and Modelo). They close with thoughts on corporate social stances and a study on consumer motivations for boycott participation, followed by a listener email about Styrofoam recycling.

entities.name: North Carolina Public Facilities Privacy and Security Act

segments.title: Opening banter on boycotts
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode on boycotts, joking about how often they are called for today and noting that caring about causes is good, while calls made without planning can be knee-jerk.

segments.title: Charles Boycott and the origin of the word
segments.summary: Charles Cunningham Boycott, an English land agent in County Mayo, Ireland, in 1879 faced a campaign by the Land League that shunned him, ruined his business, and required British-funded Northern Irish loyalists to harvest his potatoes. Father O'Malley first used boycott as a verb, and James Redpath's writing helped spread the tactic, with over a thousand boycotts in Ireland the following year.

segments.title: What makes a boycott effective
segments.summary: The hosts outline factors for an effective boycott: a clear and narrow goal, awareness and education, broad support, reaching core customers rather than non-customers, substitutability, and hitting the bottom line, which social media has changed by allowing bad press to matter quickly.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the historical section.

segments.title: Colonial boycotts, Free Produce Movement and Montgomery bus boycott
segments.summary: The hosts cover colonial boycotts against the Stamp Act and Townsend Act, the tea tax and the Boston Tea Party, and the First Continental Congress trade ban. They then discuss the Quaker Free Produce Movement against goods made by enslaved people, and the Montgomery bus boycott, which lasted 382 days until the Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional. The United Farm Workers grape boycott led by Cesar Chavez is also mentioned, with its use of bumper stickers.

segments.title: Anti-apartheid boycotts, Sun City and the US sanctions
segments.summary: The hosts describe South African apartheid and the international boycott against it, including the ANC's call for a boycott, the International Table Tennis Federation and IOC actions, British sports protests, US college divestment, the Sun City song and album by Artists United Against Apartheid, and the Congress override of Reagan's veto of sanctions. They note the fall of the Berlin Wall and Mandela's release as part of the broader pressure.

segments.title: North Carolina bathroom bill boycott
segments.summary: The 2016 North Carolina Public Facilities Privacy and Security Act, known as the Bathroom Bill, prompted a viral social media boycott. Corporations, entertainers, movie studios and the NCAA and NBA responded, and the hosts say the state lost about 3.76 billion dollars in the year the bill was in effect before it was repealed in 2017.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the discussion of social media boycotts.

segments.title: Social media boycotts and buycotts: Goya and Nike
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how social media makes boycotts fast and frequent and how news covers them. They examine the Goya boycott after its CEO praised Donald Trump, which led to a conservative buycott and a temporary sales bump, and the Nike boycott and buycott after its Colin Kaepernick ad, which the hosts say boosted Nike sales.

segments.title: Bud Light boycott and Modelo
segments.summary: After transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney's promotion with a Bud Light can, conservatives called for a boycott. Bud Light sales fell, and Modelo Especial gained, though both brands share an owner. The hosts discuss substitutability and observability, noting that public consumption affects boycott behavior.

segments.title: Corporate social stances and consumer motivations
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the value of corporate stances, the danger of taking a stand and then backpedaling, and survey data on whether consumers expect companies to address social concerns. They also cover the risk of boycott complacency and a 2004 study by Jill Klein and Andrew John on four motivators: egregiousness, efficacy, self-enhancement, and estimated participation of others.

segments.title: Expert correspondence on boycott motivations
segments.summary: The hosts describe the four motivators from the 2004 study, and that Jill Klein confirmed by email that they still apply. Josh says he consulted her and her co-author Andrew John.

segments.title: Listener mail: Styrofoam recycling
segments.summary: A listener named Matt, who runs Rekindle Candle Company in Georgia, writes about recycling. He says his shop recycles most of its waste and that the Charm recycling center told him low density plastic and Styrofoam are sold to a company that makes synthetic decking.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck thank listeners and the production team, and the episode closes with the standard iHeartRadio credits.
